data.html:
Lesson Overview

This is the final major lesson in your Mousetrap Build course — and it's one of the most important. In the previous lesson, you explored salvage value and resource recovery, learning how the parts in your mousetrap car still hold worth even after their primary use. Today, that groundwork pays off as you step into the "Death & Recycling" phase of the Creationeering™ framework.

Closing a project is more than just taking your car apart. It's a systematic process of decommissioning, disassembling, and honestly evaluating everything you built — from your earliest design sketches to your final performance runs. Every decision you made along the way shapes how this project ends, and how responsibly you handle those materials and lessons matters. This is stewardship in action.

Learning Objectives

Students will:

  • Understand the Creationeering™ "Death & Recycling" phase as it applies to project closure.
  • Learn systematic methods for decommissioning and disassembling a mousetrap car safely and efficiently.
  • Identify opportunities for recycling, reusing, and repurposing components from their mousetrap car.
  • Develop a critical approach to evaluating project outcomes and documenting lessons learned.
  • Recognize the biblical principle of stewardship in the responsible handling of materials at the end of a project.

data.html:
The Potter's Hand

Before we look at tools and checklists, let's anchor this phase in something bigger. In Jeremiah 18, God tells the prophet to go down to a potter's house and watch. The potter is working at the wheel, and the vessel he's shaping gets spoiled — it doesn't come out right. So what does the potter do? He doesn't throw the clay away. He reworks it. He reshapes it into a new vessel, just as it seems good to him to do.

Then God says something remarkable: "Can I not do with you as this potter does?" The clay isn't wasted. The process isn't over. It simply takes a new form.

Jeremiah 18:3–6 — "So I went down to the potter's house, and there he was working at his wheel. And the vessel he was making of clay was spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworked it into another vessel, as it seemed good to the potter to do. Then the word of the Lord came to me: 'O house of Israel, can I not do with you as this potter does?' declares the Lord."

That image — clay being reshaped rather than discarded — is the perfect lens for the "Death & Recycling" phase of Creationeering™. When your mousetrap car reaches its end-of-life, the project closes, but the materials and the lessons don't disappear. Like clay in the potter's hands, they can be reworked into something new. God, the ultimate engineer and designer, models a process of repurposing and renewal. Your job, as a responsible Creationeer, is to do the same.

What Does "Closing a Project" Actually Mean?

In professional engineering, projects don't just stop — they are closed. There's a real difference. Stopping means you walk away. Closing means you follow a deliberate process to wrap things up properly. Think of it like a pilot completing a post-flight checklist after landing. The plane is on the ground, but the work isn't done until every system has been checked and logged.

Closing your mousetrap car project involves three overlapping stages:

  • Decommissioning — formally ending the car's active life and preparing it for disassembly.
  • Disassembly — carefully taking the car apart, component by component, in a way that preserves as much material value as possible.
  • Evaluation — reviewing what worked, what didn't, and documenting lessons learned for the next project.

Each stage is intentional. Each stage matters. Skipping one is like a builder tearing down a structure without checking for salvageable materials — you lose value that didn't have to be lost.

data.html:
Decommissioning Your Mousetrap Car

Decommissioning is the formal decision that a project has ended its active service. For your mousetrap car, this happens when testing and performance evaluations are complete and you've received the go-ahead to close out the build.

Before you touch a single screw, take a moment to document the car's final state. That means:

  • Photographing the car from multiple angles.
  • Recording any final performance measurements (distance traveled, speed, consistency).
  • Noting any visible damage, wear, or modifications made during the build.

This documentation is your project's closing record — the engineering equivalent of a final report. It captures what the design actually became, not just what you planned on paper. Future you (or a future teammate) will thank you for it.

Disassembling Safely and Smartly

Once the car is documented, it's time to take it apart — but carefully. Disassembly isn't demolition. A good engineer disassembles the way a surgeon operates: methodically, purposefully, and with respect for what's in front of them.

Here's a smart approach to disassembling your mousetrap car:

  • Work in reverse order of assembly. The last thing you attached is usually the first thing you remove.
  • Sort components as you go. Separate parts into categories: reuse, recycle, and discard. Don't mix them in a pile.
  • Handle the mousetrap mechanism carefully. Even a spent mousetrap can snap and cause injury. Treat it with caution.
  • Keep hardware together. Screws, nuts, axles, and bolts are often the most reusable components. Keep them in a labeled container.
  • Inspect each part as you remove it. Is it damaged? Still functional? Could it work in another project?

Safety first: Always treat the mousetrap spring mechanism as potentially loaded, even after use. Keep fingers away from the snap bar and release the spring fully before disassembly. A snap at the wrong moment can cause a real injury.

Recycling, Reusing, and Repurposing

Once your car is disassembled and sorted, you're ready to make real stewardship decisions about each component. The three pathways are recycling, reusing, and repurposing — and they're not the same thing.

  • Recycling means the material gets broken down and turned into something entirely new — like melting aluminum axles to be used in a future project or returning foam to a materials bin.
  • Reusing means a component goes directly back into service in the same form — a working wheel that gets saved for the next build, for example.
  • Repurposing is the most creative option. It means taking a component and adapting it for a completely different use. A long wooden dowel from your car frame might become a structural element in a bridge build.

This is where the potter's clay image comes to life in practical engineering. Nothing has to be wasted. The question is just: what does this piece become next?

data.html:
Evaluating Your Project: Lessons Learned

Here's the part that separates good engineers from great ones: honest evaluation. After all the physical work of closing your project, you need to close the intellectual loop too. That means sitting down — individually or as a team — and asking hard questions about how the project went.

A solid lessons-learned review covers three areas:

  • What worked well? Identify design choices, materials, or processes that performed better than expected. These are worth repeating.
  • What didn't work? Be specific. Not "the wheels were bad" but "the axle-to-wheel friction was too high because we used tape instead of a proper sleeve." Precision in your critique leads to better solutions next time.
  • What would you do differently? This is the forward-looking question. It turns a past project into a springboard for future improvement.

A life cycle assessment — looking at the full journey of your car from raw materials to final disassembly — can also reveal patterns you didn't notice during the build. Where did you use the most materials? Where did you create the most waste? These are questions engineers ask about real products every day.

Write it down. Your lessons-learned notes are only useful if they exist somewhere you can find them. Keep a project journal or fill out your close-out documentation sheet completely. The insight that feels obvious today is easy to forget six months from now when you're starting a new build.

Stewardship as an Engineering Discipline

Everything you've done in this closing phase — documenting, disassembling carefully, sorting materials, evaluating honestly — is an expression of stewardship. Stewardship is a biblical principle, but it's also a professional engineering standard. Companies that manage the end-of-life of their products well save money, reduce waste, and build reputations for responsibility.

As a Creationeer, you're learning to hold both of those things at once. You honor God by caring for what He made. And you honor the craft of engineering by refusing to cut corners — even when the project is over and no one is grading the cleanup.

That's the full picture of the Creationeering™ life cycle: from the first idea sketched on paper, through design and testing, all the way to the final sorting of parts. Every phase matters. Every phase reflects who you are as a builder, a thinker, and a steward.

data.title: Going Deeper: Life Cycle Assessment in Real Engineering
data.html:
Professional engineers use a formal tool called a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) to measure the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction all the way through disposal or recycling. An LCA tracks things like energy used, water consumed, carbon emitted, and waste generated at every stage.

For example, when a car manufacturer designs a new vehicle, they run an LCA to understand not just how efficient the car is while driving, but how much energy it takes to build it and what happens to the materials when the car is retired after 15 years.

Your mousetrap car is a miniature version of that same challenge. What materials did you use? Where did they come from? Where do they go when you're done? Even a small project like this can teach you to think in full life cycles — a skill that will serve you in every engineering project you ever take on.
